summary: Psalm 62 moves between personal trust, pressure from attackers, and public instruction. The speaker begins and returns to the claim that God alone is his rock, salvation, fortress, and refuge, then warns the people not to trust status, oppression, robbery, or riches. The final lines ground that warning in God's power, loving kindness, and judgment according to each person's work.
whyItMatters: This psalm is a compact example of how Psalms can turn private confidence into instruction for a community. It places human threats and human wealth on one side, and God's power and refuge on the other.

context.author: The heading says, “A Psalm by David,” while Davidic headings may indicate authorship, association, dedication, or belonging; readers differ on how much the heading establishes.
context.audience: Israel's worshiping and instructed community, with later Jewish and Christian communities also receiving the Psalms for public prayer and private life.
context.date: The Psalms were composed and collected over time; the exact date of Psalm 62 is uncertain.
context.setting: Psalm 62 belongs to Book II of Psalms, a section containing Korahite, Asaphite, and Davidic material. The poem itself names attack, deception, social rank, riches, and trust in God, but does not give a specific historical event.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew poetry and prayer, with repetition, images of refuge and stability, direct address to the speaker's own soul, and communal instruction.

outline.heading: Trust stated in God alone
outline.note: The speaker says his soul rests in God, who is his salvation, rock, and fortress.

outline.heading: Attack and deception named
outline.note: The speaker addresses those trying to bring a man down and describes their lies and divided speech.

outline.heading: Trust repeated and widened
outline.note: The speaker tells his soul to wait for God, repeats the rock and fortress language, and calls the people to trust and pour out their hearts before God.

outline.heading: False securities rejected
outline.note: The poem weighs human status, oppression, robbery, and riches, and warns against setting the heart on them.

outline.heading: God's power and kindness
outline.note: The closing lines say power belongs to God, loving kindness belongs to the Lord, and each person is rewarded according to work.

keyVerses.text: For the Chief Musician. To Jeduthun. A Psalm by David. My soul rests in God alone. My salvation is from him.
keyVerses.why: This opening introduces the psalm's central posture: the speaker locates rest and salvation in God alone.

keyVerses.text: He alone is my rock and my salvation, my fortress. I will not be shaken.
keyVerses.why: This repeats and sharpens the stability language from the beginning, making God the source of security against pressure.

keyVerses.text: Trust in him at all times, you people. Pour out your heart before him. God is a refuge for us. Selah.
keyVerses.why: The psalm turns from the speaker's own trust to a direct invitation for the people to trust God and speak openly before him.

keyVerses.text: Also to you, Lord, belongs loving kindness, for you reward every man according to his work.
keyVerses.why: The final verse holds together God's loving kindness and God's judgment, preventing the psalm's trust from becoming vague optimism.

themes: Power and loving kindness belonging to God

questions.question: Who is speaking in this psalm?
questions.answer: The heading identifies it as “A Psalm by David,” but such headings can indicate authorship, association, dedication, or belonging. The poem itself speaks in the first person and also addresses attackers and the people. A reader can follow the voice of the poem without settling every historical question about its first setting.

questions.question: What does it mean that the soul “rests” or waits for God?
questions.answer: In this chapter, the phrase describes the speaker's settled reliance on God rather than on attackers, status, force, theft, or wealth. Verse 5 gives a close parallel: “My soul, wait in silence for God alone.” The point is not passivity about everything, but where the speaker places expectation and security.

questions.question: Why does the psalm repeat “He alone is my rock” language?
questions.answer: The repetition is part of the poem's structure. Verses 2 and 6 both call God the speaker's rock, salvation, and fortress, while verses 5-7 expand the claim after the description of attack. The repeated language lets the reader hear trust reasserted after pressure is named.

questions.question: Who are the attackers in verses 3-4?
questions.answer: The psalm does not name them. It describes them as people who assault a man, intend to throw him down from his lofty place, delight in lies, and speak blessing outwardly while cursing inwardly. The lack of names makes the pressure vivid without tying it to one recoverable event.

questions.question: What is “Selah”?
questions.answer: “Selah” appears at the end of verses 4 and 8. It is an uncertain musical or performance marker whose exact instruction is no longer known. It signals something about how the poem was transmitted for voiced or musical use, but readers should not pretend certainty about the precise effect.

questions.question: Is verse 9 saying people do not matter?
questions.answer: No. The verse compares human rank and reliability with God as refuge and power. “Men of low degree” are called “just a breath,” and “men of high degree” are “a lie,” which undercuts confidence in social status rather than denying human worth. The surrounding verses warn against trusting people, wealth, or coercive power as ultimate security.

questions.question: Why does the psalm warn against oppression, robbery, and riches together?
questions.answer: Verse 10 rejects both violent or dishonest gain and the subtler confidence that can come when riches increase. The psalm treats these as rival places to set the heart. That warning fits the wider movement from false supports to God as refuge.

questions.question: How can God reward every person according to work and still be described with loving kindness?
questions.answer: The final verse places both claims side by side: loving kindness belongs to the Lord, and he rewards every person according to work. Readers differ on how to relate divine kindness and judgment in broader theology, but this chapter does not separate them. It presents God's rule as both powerful and morally responsive.

glossary.def: A phrase in the heading that points to the psalm's use in a performed or musical setting, though the exact ancient practice is uncertain.
A name in the heading. In this chapter it marks an association for the psalm, but the heading does not explain the person or role further.
A preserved performance term in verses 4 and 8. Its exact meaning is uncertain, so it is best read as a marker within the poem rather than translated into a precise instruction.
An image for secure protection. The speaker uses it for God in verses 2 and 6 while describing pressure from people who want to bring him down.
Scales for weighing. Verse 9 uses the image to say that human status, whether low or high, proves lighter than a breath when weighed as a source of security.
